analysis: A Jaeger-LeCoultre Atmos mantel clock at $400-600 is inside the band and is a genuinely clever object -- it runs on the expansion of a gas bellows driven by ambient temperature change, so it never needs winding. Six photographs suggests the movement and case are being shown.
problems: Atmos clocks are common (hundreds of thousands were made) and the market reflects that. The real risk is condition: the bellows perish, the suspension wire is fragile, and a non-running Atmos costs $600-1,200 to service properly -- more than the clock. Confirm it is running and the glass panels are uncracked, or treat it as a $150 object.
patience: High. Atmos clocks appear constantly and non-runners are abundant.

melt.basis: ring mount; the palladium portion is not costed

gems.note: A diamond solitaire carrying nearly all the value, with no carat weight, colour or clarity stated.

analysis: A vintage 14K yellow gold, palladium and diamond solitaire ring. The gold is $225-450; the $4,000-6,000 estimate is the diamond.
problems: Out of band, and an undocumented solitaire. Note the brief's warning about diamond solitaires being outside this budget entirely -- this run confirms it.

gems.note: Emerald and diamond. Emeralds are almost universally oiled or resin-treated; disclosure is rare and treatment materially affects value.

analysis: A vintage 18K gold, emerald and diamond ring. Gold is $385-770 against a $2,000-3,000 estimate, so the emerald carries it.
problems: Out of band. Emeralds are also the most fragile of the major gemstones -- included, oiled and prone to chipping at the girdle. Check the stone under magnification for surface-reaching fractures.

melt.note: Platinum -- no working rate in the brief, and poor scrap recovery.

gems.note: Diamonds and emeralds in a period Deco bracelet. As a coherent set they carry more than the sum of individual small stones would.

analysis: A genuine Art Deco platinum, diamond and emerald bracelet -- the best piece of authentic period Deco jewellery in the sale, and an honest criterion-three hit on style.
problems: Out of band at $3,500-5,000. Worth seeing at preview because it shows what real Deco looks like, which calibrates you against the revival pieces. Platinum Deco bracelets are also brittle at the links after a century.

gems.note: Undocumented solitaire diamond.

analysis: A vintage 14K gold diamond solitaire ring, $1,000-2,000. Gold is only $225-375, so this is the diamond and nothing else.
problems: Straddles the band at the low end but the estimate range is wide precisely because the stone is unspecified. Do not buy an undocumented solitaire on a hunch.
patience: Very high. Solitaire rings are the most abundant lot type in any jewellery section.

melt.basis: Golden Ellipse case; the movement is not gold

analysis: A Patek Philippe Golden Ellipse in 18K. Patek is the one name in this sale where the watch is worth far more than its gold -- roughly $1,930 to $3,090 of metal against an $8,000-15,000 estimate, and the difference is entirely brand and movement.
problems: Eight to fifteen thousand dollars is eight to fifteen times the ceiling. At this level authentication matters absolutely: confirm the movement caliber, the case and movement serials agree, and ideally that an extract from the archives exists. Redialled and re-cased Pateks are a real problem.
patience: Not applicable -- far out of band.

melt.basis: fob mount; the carnelian intaglio is stone

gems.note: A carved carnelian seal. The intaglio carving is the interest -- if the arms or device can be identified the piece gains a history, which is the only thing that lifts it above metal.

analysis: An 18K gold and carnelian watch fob seal. Genuinely antique by form and one of the few pieces in this run that would satisfy the age criterion. The gold is roughly $770 to $1,350 against a $1,500-1,600 estimate.
problems: Out of band, just. Worth noting as the closest miss in the antique-plus-gold intersection -- if it opened lower it would be worth a bid.
patience: Moderate. Georgian and Victorian fob seals appear regularly and are often cheaper than this.

melt.basis: Day-Date case and President bracelet in solid 18K -- these are genuinely heavy

analysis: A men's Rolex 18K Day-Date. The gold alone is roughly $7,700 to $12,500, which is most of the $10,000-14,000 estimate -- a reminder that at $4,000 gold a solid-gold Rolex is substantially a bullion object with a watch attached.
problems: Far out of band. Also the most counterfeited watch configuration in existence; aftermarket diamond dials and bezels are rampant and materially reduce value.
patience: Not applicable -- far out of band.

melt.basis: Cellini case and gold bracelet if present

analysis: A lady's 18K Rolex Cellini. Gold is roughly $2,400 to $3,860 against a $5,000-7,000 estimate. The Cellini is Rolex's dress line and the least sought-after part of their output, so the premium over metal is thinner than the name suggests.
problems: Out of band. Cellini resale is notably weaker than sports Rolex -- the market wants Submariners and Daytonas, not dress watches, which is why my resale figure sits close to the metal.

melt.note: Two-tone means steel with gold-plated or gold-capped elements. No meaningful melt floor.

analysis: A two-tone Breitling Chronomat. A real watch with a real movement, but two-tone steel-and-gold sports watches are the weakest configuration in the vintage market -- the taste has moved decisively to full steel.
problems: Out of band at $2,500-4,000, and my market read is below the house's. Check the chronograph functions actually work; Breitling service is expensive.

gems.note: A 3.11 carat diamond -- the only stone in the sale with a stated weight, which is itself telling. Secondary-market recovery on a stone this size is typically 30-45% of retail replacement, and colour and clarity (unstated) swing it by a factor of three.

analysis: A 14K gold and 3.11 carat diamond solitaire ring. The largest stone in the sale and the only one the house has bothered to weigh.
problems: Fifteen to eighteen thousand dollars, which is fifteen times the ceiling. Even here the catalogue gives weight but no colour or clarity grade -- at this level that omission is significant, because a 3.11ct stone can be worth $6,000 or $40,000 depending on those two letters.
patience: Not applicable -- far out of band.

analysis: A Seiko 6105 'Captain Willard' dive watch -- the model worn in Apocalypse Now, which is where the nickname and most of the value come from. Genuine cult status and a strong market among vintage-Seiko collectors.
problems: Out of band at $2,000-3,000. These are also heavily re-parted: aftermarket bezels, hands, crowns and especially redialled examples are the norm rather than the exception, and originality is most of the value. Not a criteria fit in any case.

gems.note: A 2.75 carat diamond. Same point as 3191 -- weight stated, colour and clarity not, and those determine most of the value.

analysis: A 14K gold and 2.75 carat diamond ring, the second-largest stated stone in the sale.
problems: Far out of band at $10,000-12,000. Same disclosure gap as 3191.
patience: Not applicable -- far out of band.

melt.basis: solid 14K pocket watch case; movement, dial and crystal are not gold. Confirm SOLID rather than filled -- see lot 3096, which is the gold-filled trap in the same section.

analysis: A 14K gold E. Howard pocket watch with a WWI presentation inscription. Three things converge here: a first-rank American maker, a solid gold case worth roughly $1,880 to $3,000, and a dated historical inscription that makes it a documented object rather than an anonymous watch.
problems: Out of band at $1,500-3,000, though the low end is only just past it. The presentation inscription is the interesting part -- read it at preview, because a named recipient who can be researched adds real interest. Confirm the case is solid: 'gold filled' would cut the value by two thirds.
patience: Moderate. Presentation-inscribed gold Howards are genuinely uncommon; this is the near-miss of the section.

gems.note: A single unspecified diamond, probably modest.

analysis: A 14K gold and diamond pendant necklace at $700-900 -- inside the band. The gold is only about $225 to $450, so unlike 3069 the metal does not cover the estimate and you would be paying for an undocumented diamond.
problems: One photograph and no stone detail. My market read is below the house's. Buy only well under the low estimate, and treat the diamond as worth nothing until you have looked at it.

analysis: An Omega 18K dual-register chronograph. Vintage Omega chronographs are a genuinely strong market and this one is estimated $1,000-1,600 against roughly $1,740 to $2,700 of gold -- which means the estimate sits below the metal, and my market read is well above the house's.
problems: Out of band, but only just at the low end, and this is the sort of mispricing worth knowing about: at $1,000 hammer it is $1,320 all-in against $1,700-plus of gold before the watch counts. If your budget ever flexed, this is where I would spend it. Confirm the case is solid 18K and the movement is the original caliber.
patience: Low. Underpriced vintage Omega chronographs do not sit around.

melt.note: Platinum -- no working rate, poor scrap recovery.

gems.note: Early Deco diamonds, likely old European cuts, which are increasingly sought after in their own right.

analysis: An early Art Deco platinum and diamond ring -- authentic period work, and old European cut diamonds have appreciated as a category because the cutting is warmer than modern brilliants.
problems: Out of band at $4,000-5,000. Brittle platinum mount; check the shoulders for hairlines.

melt.basis: solid 18K case; movement, dial and crystal excluded. IWC De Luxe cases of this era are solid, not plated -- but confirm the hallmark, because that is the whole argument.

analysis: This is the most underpriced lot in the jewellery and watch run. An International Watch Co. 18K automatic De Luxe estimated $800-1,500 with the bidding at $275 -- and on my weight estimate the gold case alone holds roughly $1,740 to $2,700. The metal is worth more than the top of the house estimate, and IWC movements of this period are excellent in their own right. At $800 hammer that is $1,056 all-in against $1,700-plus of gold.
problems: Only one photograph, which is poor disclosure for a gold watch -- so the case hallmark and the weight both need confirming at preview, and the whole case collapses if it turns out to be gold-capped rather than solid. Check the movement runs and is the original IWC caliber. The low current bid suggests nobody has done this arithmetic; do not assume that lasts once the room sees gold.
patience: Low. A solid-gold Swiss watch estimated below its own melt is a pricing error, not a recurring opportunity.
sources: Case weight is my estimate from the model type, not a catalogued figure. The gold rate is the brief's conservative $4,000/ozt working spot.

gems.note: Two diamonds, unspecified.

analysis: A vintage 14K gold two-diamond bypass ring. Gold is $300-530 against a $2,000-2,500 estimate, so the stones carry it and they are undocumented.
problems: Out of band and undocumented.

melt.basis: solid 14K case; movement, dial and crystal excluded. Confirm solid rather than gold-filled -- Omega used both.

analysis: The second underpriced gold watch in the run, on the same logic as 3198. A 14K Omega De Ville estimated $800-1,500 with bidding at $250, and the case holds roughly $1,130 to $1,880 of gold. The De Ville is Omega's dress line and unfashionable, which is exactly why it is cheap -- but gold does not care about fashion.
problems: The solid-versus-filled question is decisive and the catalogue does not answer it. Two photographs only. Look for '14K' alone on the caseback versus '14K gold filled' or a '1/20' fraction. If filled, this is a $200 watch. Also confirm the movement runs.
patience: Low to moderate. Gold dress watches are common, but ones bidding at a quarter of their melt are not.
sources: Case weight estimated from the model type; not catalogued.

gems.note: Tanzanite is a single-source stone that has fallen substantially from its 1990s peak; recovery is poor. The diamonds are accents.

analysis: A vintage 14K gold, tanzanite and diamond ring. Gold is $225-450 against $1,000-2,000, so the tanzanite carries it -- and tanzanite is a weak resale species.
problems: Straddles the band at the very low end. My market read is under the house's because tanzanite has not held its value.

melt.note: Hamilton Cross Country models were produced in both solid 14K and gold-filled cases. Assume filled -- and therefore no melt floor -- until the caseback proves otherwise.

analysis: A Hamilton Cross Country, estimated $800-1,000 and inside the band at the low end. Hamilton's mid-century American models have a devoted collecting base and the asymmetric-case designs of that era are the sought-after ones.
problems: The case material is the question, exactly as with 3198 and 3200 but with the answer more likely to be 'filled'. Also check the dial has not been refinished -- redialled Hamiltons are common and a refinished dial halves the value to collectors. My market range is wide because both of those are unresolved.
patience: Moderate. Hamilton dress watches are plentiful; the good asymmetric models less so.

gems.note: Rubies of unstated origin and treatment; assume treated.

analysis: A pair of 14K yellow gold ruby earrings. Gold is $375-675 against a $1,000-1,500 estimate.
problems: Marginal on band at the low estimate. Ruby treatment undisclosed.

analysis: A Patek Philippe 18K Calatrava -- the archetypal dress watch. Gold is roughly $1,740 to $2,900; the rest of the $6,000-10,000 estimate is Patek.
problems: Far out of band. Same authentication requirements as 3185: movement caliber, matching serials, archive extract ideally.
patience: Not applicable -- far out of band.

melt.basis: locket body less the enamel and glazing

gems.note: No stones. The painted enamel portrait is the interest and cannot be valued as material.

analysis: An antique 14K gold enamelled portrait locket pendant. Genuinely period, and enamel portrait lockets are a proper Victorian collecting category. The gold is roughly $600 to $1,050 against a $1,000-1,500 estimate.
problems: Out of band, just. Enamel losses are the killer here -- check the portrait for chips and hairlines, because enamel restoration is specialist and rarely invisible. Also confirm whether the portrait is painted enamel or a printed transfer under glass, which is much commoner and much cheaper.

analysis: A vintage Breitling Top Time chronograph. A genuinely collected reference with a strong following -- the Top Time is one of the more desirable 1960s Breitlings.
problems: Out of band at $3,000-4,000, and no criteria fit. Vintage chronographs are also heavily re-parted; original dials, hands and pushers are most of the value.

melt.basis: white gold ring mount, stone deducted

gems.note: Blue topaz is one of the cheapest stones in commercial jewellery -- abundant, routinely irradiated to produce the colour, and worth very little on resale.

analysis: A vintage Gucci 18K white gold and blue topaz ring. Gold is $580-1,060; the Gucci name is the premium, since the topaz is worth almost nothing.
problems: Out of band at $1,500-2,500. Designer-branded jewellery also depends entirely on the mark being right, and Gucci is widely counterfeited.

melt.note: Case material unstated. Ebel's lady's watches were made in steel, two-tone and solid gold -- if this one is gold there is a melt floor, and if it is steel there is none. The catalogue does not say.

analysis: A lady's Ebel wristwatch at $600-800, inside the band. Ebel is a respectable second-tier Swiss house and the Sport Classic 'wave' bracelet is their recognisable design.
problems: One photograph and no case material, no model, no movement type. My market range runs from $250 to $700 purely because of that. Lady's quartz watches also have the weakest resale of any watch category. Establish the case metal first; if steel, this is a $250 lot.
patience: Very high. Lady's dress watches are the most abundant and least wanted watch category.

melt.basis: 14K portions only; the platinum top is not costed as the brief gives no platinum rate

gems.note: Small Deco diamonds, likely old European or transitional cuts set in the platinum front.

analysis: An Art Deco platinum, 14K gold and diamond bar brooch at $800-1,200 -- the only genuinely period Deco jewellery in the sale that comes close to the budget. Bar brooches are the entry point to real Deco: the same design vocabulary as the expensive bracelets, at a fraction of the money, because bar brooches are less wearable today.
problems: Only just inside the band at the low estimate. The mixed platinum-and-gold construction means you cannot weigh the metals separately, so the melt figure is indicative only. Check the pin and catch and look for hairlines in the platinum gallery -- and confirm it is period rather than a 1980s Deco-revival piece, which is the standing distinction the brief insists on.
patience: Moderate. Deco bar brooches are the affordable corner of a strong style.

analysis: A Foster Campos banjo clock in the Aaron Willard style. Campos was a respected Massachusetts reproduction clockmaker, so this is a well-made modern object -- but the catalogue's own word is 'style', which per the standing principles means the cataloguer is declining to commit to a period, and here it is committing to the opposite: this is a 20th-century reproduction of a Federal form.
problems: Out of band at $1,000-1,500 and, more to the point, it fails the antique criterion by design rather than by uncertainty. Reproduction furniture and clocks by named modern makers also have weak resale -- the market pays for period or it pays very little.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band and out of criteria.

melt.basis: sculptural belt buckle in 22K -- Jean Mahie's work is characteristically massive and solid

analysis: A Jean Mahie 22K gold sculptural belt buckle, the first of five consecutive Mahie lots (3224-3228). Mahie is a genuinely collected French studio-jewellery name and the work is unmistakable -- heavy, textured, deliberately primitive. At 22K the gold runs $117.93 a gram, so 55 to 85 grams is roughly $6,500 to $10,000, meaning the metal alone covers or exceeds the $6,000-8,000 estimate.
problems: Far out of band. Worth recording that all five Mahie lots are essentially gold-backed at these estimates -- unusual in a jewellery section where most lots trade well above metal.

analysis: A Jean Mahie 22K gold link necklace. Roughly $5,900 to $9,400 of gold against a $6,000-8,000 estimate -- metal-backed, same as the rest of the group.
problems: Far out of band.

analysis: A Jean Mahie 22K gold pendant. Roughly $5,300 to $8,300 of gold against $5,500-7,000.
problems: Far out of band.

analysis: A Jean Mahie 22K gold mask pendant. Roughly $4,100 to $6,800 of gold against $4,500-5,500.
problems: Far out of band.

gems.note: Small accent diamonds only.

analysis: A pair of Jean Mahie 22K gold and diamond earclips -- the cheapest of the five Mahie lots. Roughly $3,300 to $5,300 of gold against $3,500-4,500.
problems: Far out of band, though it is the closest of the group.

melt.basis: locket body less enamel and glazing

gems.note: No stones. The plique-a-jour or champleve enamel is the value and is not recoverable as material.

analysis: This is the most frustrating lot in the sale. An Art Nouveau 14K gold enamelled moth photo locket brooch is a textbook criterion-three hit -- genuine period Nouveau, not revival, with the insect iconography that defines the style at its best -- and it is comfortably antique. The gold is roughly $580 to $1,060 against a $1,500-1,800 estimate.
problems: Out of band at $1,500-1,800 with a $750 opening, so it is $1,980 to $2,376 all-in. It is the single best fit to the buyer's stated Art Nouveau interest anywhere in 1,500 lots and it sits just past the ceiling. If the budget were ever going to flex for one lot on criteria grounds rather than value grounds, this is that lot. Check the enamel for losses, which is where these fail.
patience: Low. Genuine period Nouveau enamel at under $2,000 is not a regular occurrence at Thomaston.

melt.note: Platinum -- no working rate, poor scrap recovery.

gems.note: Emerald-cut diamond three-stone. Emerald cuts show inclusions more readily than brilliants, so clarity matters more than usual -- and it is unstated.

analysis: A vintage platinum emerald-cut diamond three-stone ring, the fourth of the near-identical three-stone group.
problems: Out of band and undocumented as to stones.

gems.note: Unspecified diamonds.

analysis: A 14K gold and diamond ring with no further description -- five photographs but no stone data. Gold is $300-600 against $3,000-4,000.
problems: Out of band. The pattern across this whole consignment is consistent: four-figure estimates resting on stones the catalogue never specifies.

gems.note: Garnet and mabe pearl. Garnet is inexpensive; mabe (blister) pearls are assembled half-domes and the cheapest pearl product there is.

analysis: A 14K gold garnet and mabe pearl bracelet. The gold is roughly $900 to $1,500, which is most of the $1,500-2,000 estimate -- the stones contribute very little.
problems: Out of band. Mabe pearls also delaminate and the domes crack, which is not repairable.

gems.note: Emerald, sapphire and diamond in one ring -- a 'cocktail' combination where the stones are typically small, treated and commercial-grade.

analysis: A 14K gold emerald, sapphire and diamond ring. Gold is $300-530 against $1,000-1,500.
problems: Marginal on band at the low estimate. Multi-stone cocktail rings are where the least valuable material in the trade ends up -- three stone species in one modest ring is a signal, not a feature.

melt.basis: two-tone floral link bracelet -- substantial gold

analysis: A 14K two-tone gold floral link bracelet with no stones, which makes it the purest metal lot in the run: roughly $2,100 to $3,390 of gold against a $3,000-4,000 estimate.
problems: Out of band. With no stones and no maker, this will trade close to metal -- which also means it is one of the few lots here whose value is genuinely predictable.

gems.note: Multi-colour sapphires -- fancy-colour sapphire is abundant and frequently heat-treated or synthetic in this class.

analysis: A John C. Rinker 14K gold multi-colour sapphire and diamond ring. Rinker is a minor contemporary maker, so the signature adds little. Gold is $300-600 against $1,000-1,500.
problems: Marginal on band at the low end. Multi-colour sapphire suites are a commercial product rather than a collector one.

melt.basis: figaro link chain -- chains are the most honestly weighable gold objects in any sale

analysis: An Italian 14K gold figaro link chain. No stones, no maker premium, nothing to assess but weight: roughly $1,880 to $3,010 of gold against a $1,900-2,100 estimate. This is a bullion lot in all but name and will trade within a few percent of its metal.
problems: Out of band. But this is the one lot in the section where the value is completely knowable in advance -- put it on a scale and you have the answer. Check the clasp is gold and not base metal, and that the stamp reads 14K rather than 14K GP.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band. Gold chains are always available.

gems.note: Unspecified diamonds.

analysis: A vintage 14K gold and diamond bracelet. Gold roughly $1,350 to $2,260 against $2,500-3,000.
problems: Out of band.

melt.basis: gold clasp and elements only -- the sapphire beads are the bulk and are stone, not metal

gems.note: Multi-strand sapphire beads. Bead-grade sapphire is opaque, heavily included material worth a few dollars a strand -- nothing like faceted stone. Do not let 'sapphire' in the title imply value.

analysis: A 14K gold, diamond and multi-strand sapphire bead necklace at $800-1,200, inside the band at the low end. The gold is roughly $450 to $900; the sapphire beads look impressive and are worth very little.
problems: The word 'sapphire' is doing heavy lifting here and bead-grade material is the cheapest form the species takes. Current bid is already $400. Weigh the gold and price the beads at nearly nothing.

melt.note: Case material unstated. A Datejust may be steel, two-tone or solid gold -- at this estimate probably steel or two-tone, in which case there is no meaningful melt floor.

analysis: A vintage Rolex Datejust. The most-produced Rolex reference and a reliable market, but the catalogue gives no reference number, no case material and no date.
problems: Far out of band at $8,000-10,000. Also the configuration where aftermarket dials, bezels and bracelets are most common; originality is most of the value and none of it is documented here.
patience: Not applicable -- far out of band.

melt.basis: white gold ring mount, stones deducted

gems.note: South Sea pearl and diamonds. South Sea pearls are the better end of cultured pearls and hold value rather better than akoya, but still recover poorly relative to their retail price.

analysis: An 18K white gold South Sea pearl and diamond ring. Gold is $385-770 against $1,500-1,800.
problems: Out of band. Pearl rings also wear badly -- the pearl abrades against surfaces in a way a pendant never does, so check the surface carefully.

gems.note: Unspecified diamonds.

analysis: A 14K gold and diamond ring with an interlocking loop design. Gold is $300-600 against $1,000-1,500.
problems: Marginal on band at the low end, no stone documentation.

gems.note: The turquoise intaglio is the whole question. A genuine Roman intaglio -- even a modest one -- is a two-thousand-year-old carved object worth $200-800 on its own. A modern glass or resin cast of one is worth $10. The three Windemuth lots (3243-3245) all turn on this.

analysis: An Ellen Windemuth necklace set with what is described as a Roman turquoise intaglio. Windemuth is a contemporary designer who mounts antique and ancient intaglios in modern settings -- so the mount is new and the stone may be genuinely ancient. At $300-500 this is inside the band and is the most interesting speculative lot in the jewellery run.
problems: Everything depends on whether the intaglio is ancient, an 18th-century Grand Tour copy, or a modern cast -- and all three are commonly sold as 'Roman'. Under a loupe, ancient carving shows wheel marks and wear inconsistent with modern tooling; cast glass shows bubbles and mould seams. Note also that 'Roman turquoise' is an odd combination, since turquoise intaglios are far less common than carnelian or agate. Ask the house what the attribution rests on.
patience: Moderate. Windemuth pieces appear periodically; genuine ancient intaglios at this money would be a real find.

gems.note: Scarab and centaur intaglios. The scarab is Egyptian iconography and the centaur Greek or Roman, so this is a made-up pairing of two separate stones -- which is normal for this designer but means each needs assessing separately.

analysis: The second Ellen Windemuth intaglio necklace, combining a scarab and a centaur. Same proposition as 3243: a modern setting whose value rests entirely on the age of the stones.
problems: Two stones means two authenticity questions. Egyptian scarabs are among the most reproduced antiquities in existence -- faience and steatite copies have been made continuously since the 19th century. Loupe both stones.

gems.note: Carnelian is the classic Roman intaglio material, which makes this the most plausible of the three -- most surviving genuine Roman intaglios are carnelian, agate or nicolo. That raises the odds without settling them.

analysis: The third Ellen Windemuth necklace, set with a Roman carnelian intaglio. Of the three this is the one where the stone species matches what genuine Roman intaglios are actually made from, so it is the best of the group to pursue.
problems: Same loupe test. Grand Tour intaglios of the 18th and 19th centuries were themselves carved in carnelian in deliberate imitation of Roman work and are often sold as ancient -- though a genuine Grand Tour intaglio is itself an antique by this brief's standard, which is a softer landing than a modern cast.
